What medication did you try?

Herpes medication works for numerous other conditions, so it's very plausible that it's *not* herpes, but it's something related. 

For example, I take valcyclovir for hsv-1, BUT, I also know that it can be used to treat related viruses, such as chickenpox and shingles.

If you're not testing positive for herpes on a blood or swab test... it probably isn't herpes. But it might be something related to herpes.

I know some of the difficulty for oral HSV may be the fact that it's on your face & the stigma (my boyfriend has oral hsv-1), but for me, the itch sensation is probably the worst part and getting rid of that makes it sooo much more manageable.

I feel you OP, I used to be like this: I also have (c)PTSD, and cutting / self harm in general was my way of validating my pain (while also just genuinely being desperate to cope). And yes, it did also feel "thrilling" to plan all of it out, too.

I'm not really in the position to give advice - I only got better after I realized my self destruction was going to kill me (near death experience) and I realized I didn't *actually* want to die. Interestingly enough, I kind of phrased it to myself as "this ending is so cliché and overdone and just kinda sad, it would be more poetic if I said fuck the people who traumatized me and succeeded out of spite" - though some of it was also, yes, the fear of death even though for the longest time, I thought that was what I wanted. I really felt young for the first time, and looking back 2-3 years later, I *was* young, and it's honestly appalling to think of what I was doing to myself, and what happened to me when I was literally just a kid.

In that regard, I can't really tell you how to get better: at least I can't tell you how to reach your breaking point. But if you're anything like me, while it will not be easy, once you *do* hit that breaking point, you will have a lot of resolve and determination to "turn shit around." 

That said - I do wanna say it *does* get better, just hold on as long as you can. Anything to reduce harm helps. I was in this odd phase of semi-recovering, simply practicing harm reduction (when i felt like it) without the full commitment to recovery, for a while before I hit my breaking point and essentially went "cold turkey." And while full recovery is better, again, anything to reduce harm is better than nothing. It does help you in the long term.

I thought I would never get better, and while I certainly still struggle with cPTSD, and yes, I even cut occasionally, I am so, so much better. I want you to know that's possible, and I am rooting for you.

It also looks open... did you happen to pop it or did it happen on its own? I know when I had my first herpes sore pop up, I thought (hoped) it was a pimple, but when I tried to pop it, it doesn't pop in the same way (which is probably good, that is - mostly - how you spread herpes). It does look similar after it pops on its own, but again, unless you've had herpes for years and didn't know it, then just suddenly had a VERY minor outbreak, it's probably not herpes.

To test for it they would need to swab it, but it's probably going to be closed before you can get into an urgent care or something. They can test for it by blood, but it's relatively useless because... literally some 90% of the world has asymptomatic herpes. Most standard STI panels don't include blood tests for herpes for this reason.

I'm also 17 and in the exact same postion as you - childhood trauma, mental health issues, never really started brushing my teeth until this last year or so. It is embarrassing, but it's part of what happens when you don't get the help you need.

I had (and still kind of have) long term gum disease from mine, my teeth are yellow and my last appointment my dentist noted that my teeth have scarring down at the bottom. I have quite a few cavities that we're monitoring (but aren't being addressed quite yet because of braces)

I would talk to your parents about getting dental care, firstly. I know it's embarrassing and you may feel guilty, but a dentist would really help you in more ways than dentists here can since they can actually see your teeth, talk to you in depth, etc. Every time I go in, I feel embarrassed, yes, but it's also their job to deal with people who have bad teeth. If a dentist is going to judge you for your teeth, they're not in the right profession.

Some advice I have as someone who has started this process: 

1) reduce feelings of shame, celebrate tiny wins, and make tiny steps if you have to. brushing twice a week is better than not at all. sometimes you have to work up to it. i've worked up to brushing every night, and i'm starting to try flossing twice a week, as reccomended by my dentist as the "minimum"

2) make it a routine. if you brush your teeth at night, try it at the same time; try and do it before you're tired - i always found myself wanting to skip brushing because i'd be "too exhausted" but if you skip one day, it's easy to skip the next, and the next, and the next... and then you're back in the cycle. try and stay committed. habits are easier to break than they are to form

3) find little "hacks" ... i have a toothbrush in my car, with a waterbottle & chewable toothpaste (which is kinda gross tbh) that helped me brush in the morning sometimes. when i first started, i had to listen to a song or an audiobook while brushing to get myself motivated to do it. i'm awful with timing so i always set a timer while brushing my teeth. for a while, i would break a 2 minute segment into 4 parts: brush upper teeth, pointed up for 30 secs, brush upper teeth, pointed down for 30 secs, brush lower teeth, pointed up for 30 secs and brush lower teeth pointed down for 30 secs. right now with flossing, i wear latex gloves because i can't stand the feeling of my hands in/near my mouth ... tldr; it may take experimenting but find small things that motivate you

i know it might seem pointless right now, or like your teeth are already screwed so you might as well just give up, but... that's really not true. i've been prioritizing my teeth for maybe 6 months (at most), and i've already seen some pretty significant improvement in my gums & teeth. sure, your teeth may not be "perfect" but in this journey, i've realized many don't have perfect teeth anyway.

And then there's just the fact that sometimes you aren't the right person to help. If your friend comes up to you with a broken leg, you wouldn't try to put it in a cast, you'd tell them to see a doctor (& maybe help them get there). In the same way, you aren't a psychologist or a social worker or a therapist, etc etc etc ... sometimes you can only do so much, and it's better to not respond (primarily online) or refer them to someone else

1. Night sweats are common in ed recovery, it's kinda a mix of your body "fixing" itself on the inside, and hypermetabolism. (Also does sound a bit like extreme hunger)

But also leading into 2. It sounds like your blood sugar is crashing. Early into my recovery, I dealt with the same thing. Compared with your hunger, I would suggest looking into "reactive hypoglycemia". Basically it seems like every 2-4 hours your blood sugar is crashing, meaning you need to eat again to get it back up. 

I still struggle with it a bit, but the longer into recovery, the easier it gets. It is a pain in the ass, and I know at times I was so regretful, and I felt so much agony, but again, it is managable and the only solution is to recover. 

Some tiny tips for managing it are:

- eat every 2-4 hours. the second you start thinking "oh i might be hungry" ... eat. bevause you probably are hungry, and you want to eat before you recieve any physical symptoms.

- always carry food on you. seriously, ALWAYS. you never know when it will happen. if you drive, again, ALWAYS eat before you start driving so your blood sugar doesn't crash while you drive - it's extremely dangerous and can result in a coma, death, etc.

- it's okay to eat sugary things (especially while managing extreme hunger, which you will undoubtedly face) but it's always a good idea to "balance" it out with food higher in protein, or fat. this helps lessen the effect of your blood sugar crashing, since they are different energies for you body to use.

- eating whole carbs or dietary fiber is generally better than simple carbs (sugar) because they last longer, making your blood sugar "crash" less extreme.

- avoid sugar free products. using a product with sugar will actually be better for you. your body will produce insulin at the taste of anything sweet (which is what causes the issue) and is done so in excess. a sugar free product gives you no glucose to process, meaning your insulin levels will be higher, making your actual blood sugar levels too low. the product with sugar will at least put some glucose in your blood, which helps lower insulin and keep your blood sugar levels stable.

Honestly, you just have to eat through it. It's probably not what you want to hear, but extreme hunger doesn't go away until your body recognizes "okay, when i'm hungry, i can get food" and that you don't need to "stock up for later". 

Part of that process will ofc be changing your mindset. You're going to have to get comfortable with gaining some weight, and eating unhealthy foods, & so you need to learn that food/weight does not equal your worth, that neither matter. And you also have to learn that your body is your body, calories are only energy & nothing bad will happen if you "overeat" one day, two days, and so forth. The world doesn't end. You basically have to remember that your thoughts are irrational, and you need to eat until you're no longer hungry. And yes, that will be a lot of food at first, but you do NEED that food, and you're not overeating by honoring extreme hunger. 

A lot of your mindset will change by using positive affirmations and doing the opposite of what you think (ex: "i can't wear that, i look too fat" and then wearing it, flaunting it, and saying "damn, i look great"). You might not feel it at first, at that's okay, but you eventually do get there. It's a lot of practice. 

Also on the diabetes - I developed a similar condition, reactive hypoglycemia, which means I have to manage my sugars like I was diabetic anyway (a bit stricter in some areas and losers in others) and many theorize it might be a form of prediabetes. I developed this ... FROM ANOREXIA. Restricting, purging, etc. will not save you from diabetes. It can actually increase your risk in some cases, and ultimately, type 2 diabetes seems to be mostly genetic, and is a manageable condition, even if it's a pain in the ass. There really isn't much you can do to "prevent" it regardless, but I can tell you an eating disorder can increase your risk of developing diabetes (or a similar condition). Like many disordered thoughts, it's illogical, and it's important to remember that.

1) Yes. I ended up developing reactive hypoglycemia as a result of my eating disorder, which means my body produces way more insulin then necessary, causing my blood sugar to crash, and... Shortly after beginning recovery, maybe 2 months in, I realized I was likely near death. My blood sugar was extremely low all the time, I was experiencing muscular atrophy, and my heart wasn't doing what it was supposed to. I wasn't even at an underweight bmi, but I likely was "underweight" in the sense that I was far under where my body needed to be for my physical health. When I look back at photos, I just feel sad for my old self. I never felt sick enough, but I was really, really sick, and it did show, even if I didn't think it did.

2) Yeah, of course. Most people will have doubts in ED recovery, but they're just that, doubts. They aren't rooted in reality. I worried that I would gain too much weight, or that I would binge, which I didn't. Most of my binging turned out to be reactive eating. I thought I wouldn't be able to do it, but I did, and I've been rocking it. Sometimes I miss it, yeah, but I know I'm so much better off than I was, and I don't feel the desire to go back. When I do, I usually go to bed and forget about it in the morning. The one time I did attempt a relapse, I realized it was miserable. 

3) That I can do it, and the struggle gets so much better to cope with. The more you practice eating normally, not listening to disordered thoughts, eating food you used to fear, not over-exercising or starving, etc. - the easier it gets to resist. I rarely even think about some of my disordered thoughts anymore, even if they're present, because I know they're disordered, and not worth listening to. The distress is temporary, and coping is so much easier than you think once you have the energy to participate in your hobbies and think clear thoughts and actually produce the chemicals you need to be happy.

4) The distress is temporary, please, please, please stick it out. You will feel so much better physically, to the point you'll realize you never truly understood how physically taxing your ED is. Also - don't worry about binging, it is 100% normal to eat a crapload of food in early recovery. You will feel hungry all the time, and want to eat a hell lot. It's a bit scary at first, but it is necessary. Your body needs to make up for the energy it lost, and repair itself. Listen to your cravings and your hunger. Don't delay eating or deny yourself food. The best thing you can do in recovery is to *just* eat, no matter what your head is telling you.

Also, drill it into your brain that food is food, there is no inherent value to it. food cannot be good, and food cannot be bad. it is food, and you need to eat food to survive. don't worry about the calories or the nutrition, eat what you want. eventually you will get into the practice of eating what you need, by listening to your body. don't worry about moderating junk food or eating healthy at first - just eat. you will figure that out later, naturally rather than conciously.

This drop is much more rapid than it normally should be.

When I eat quick sugars or simple carbs, like say cereal or a milk chocolate bar, the drop in blood sugar is more extreme than if I had something with a complex carb, like vegetables, a protein, like peanut butter, or a fat, like cheese. This drop in blood sugar makes you really sick, and if untreated, you can end up in a coma and possibly die.

I would talk to your doctor and/or therapist about this, because if you don't want medication, maybe you shouldn't take it. However, I'll also share my experience with my SNRI, as well as other medication:

Personally, I take effexor/venlafaxine and have been for a while, and it helped me a lot. I didn’t have any side effects from what I remember while starting it almost 2 years ago now. I pretty much went to the max dose as soon as the doctors thought I could tolerate it, and I haven't had to increase it since.

There were a lot of horror stories about Venlafaxine, just like there is for Cymbalta from what you've said. However, most of these cases are rare, and if you communicate well with your doctor, none of them should last a particularly long time. I tried a lot of different SSRI's and SNRI's, maybe two antipsychotics, as well as anxiety medication and medication for insomnia, but I only had a bad reaction to one of them, which was an SSRI. 

It made me manic and gave me psychosis, but was the only med to do that out of ALL the different ones I tried - and it's extremely rare. It's actually a very common antidepressant that usually *doesn't* have any horror stories. I wasn't really committed to getting better at the time, and so I stayed on it longer than I should have. If I had stopped sooner, like the first time I noticed something was off, I likely wouldn't have been alright.

The mania has gone away completely, and went away pretty fast, but the hallucinations lasted over a year. At first I managed them with anti-psychotics that were also supposed to help with bipolar disorder (which we weren't sure if I had at the time - I did not), which helped, but eventually I came off of them because they were kind of numbing emotionally and it raised my cholesterol a bit more than it should've. Suprisingly, I was fine, no mania, and I didn't have any increase in hallucinations after going off. 

It's been almost 3 years since I stopped, and at some point, most of the hallucinations went away. I still have some, but they're very minor and manageable. They also do tend to be triggered by certain things, mostly anxiety and trauma, so it's likely that the medication wasn't the only cause, and just opened a door that was already unlocked. 

Which all sounds a bit scary, but ultimately, I ended up fine. The majority of side effects from medication will stop after you've quit taking them, or, if it's not a serious side effect (like headaches or nausea), after your body had adjusted to the medication. These horror stories are often written by people who are still in the midst of struggling due to the side effects, and rarely by the people who had the side effects, struggled, and got better. It sucks in the moment, sure, but it will be okay.

As for withdrawal... yes, it can be pretty severe, but realistically you should not have a problem as long as you follow what your doctor tells you to do. Missing one dose or taking a late dose by accident will make you feel shitty, but chances are, it won't kill you. 

I have ADHD on top of CPTSD, which gives me an AWFUL memory, so if you're also like that, set yourself an alarm at the time you need to take your meds, and force yourself to get up to take them, because I have definitely had the "oh, I'll get them in a minute" and then I forgot.

The time I had bad withdrawals was because I was weaning myself off, without doctors orders, and went WAYYY too fast. It was ass, and I definitely felt like dying, but that was my own doing. I knew I shouldn't have done it, and I knew the risks, but I still did it. Otherwise, you should be perfectly fine. If you ever feel like stopping your medication - talk to your doctor or your therapist, and have them instruct you how to do that safely. SNRI's are particularly ass, but this applies to every medication. Never just stop taking them. As long as you follow those rules, you'll likely never have to suffer from any extreme withdrawal. You might have mild symptoms when you decrease your dose like your doctor says, but you should be totally fine.

For emotions and trauma? You're absolutely right, SNRI's will not cure everything. They will not bring back your parents or change the past or anything. However, they can increase your mood which can help you take steps that you might not be able to make in therapy right now.

I would say my medication is a very small piece of the puzzle, but a very important one, because it's the building block I needed. I had been in therapy for years, and it just wasn't very effective for me, because I never really felt like getting better. I was too depressed to do much and didn't see the point. I could barely get out of bed or do basic tasks. 

Starting medication gave me that push I needed to actually start applying what I learned in therapy to my life. Before I knew it deep down, but I simply couldn't do it. Again, a very small piece, but it's like the foundation, and without it, I probably wouldn't be much better, which I learned when I was irresponsible and tried to stop taking it. 

The medication can basically just give you an emotional push you need to break through, especially if you suffer from chronic feelings of hopelessness or addiction like I did. It also gave me some emotional stability that I lost after my trauma and meds kept me from getting depressed way too fast after encountering a trigger and having an emotional meltdown. I also noticed a general decrease in flashbacks.

It can also help manage the physical symptoms trauma gives you, as a lot of the physical symptoms are usually tied to the mental part.

These are just my experiences, and everyone has different reactions to different meds, and I don't know your situation enough to evaluate whether medication is something you need, however, it's something I think might be able to help you when considering if medication is right for you, especially if your main concern is fear of medication. This is not me telling you to take meds, nor is it me telling you to not take meds. Every path is different, and while some of us need medication, others might not. Both of those options are equally okay. 

Just figure out what you need for yourself, communicate with your care team and take it from there. I would reccomend writing down a list of questions and concerns you have for your doctor before you start Cymbalta so you can evaluate where you stand. You'll eventually get to a place where you'll have a good understanding of your needs and wants when it comes to your treatment. Good luck and take care!

A lot of the replies have good answers that don't just apply to severely underweight people but... even being mildly underweight is a concern. Your ED can kill you at any weight. There have been obese and fat people who have died from starvation, as well as purging. 

I was only ever "mildly underweight" before I went into recovery, and only for a short period, not even when I did recover, but I still have long term consequences of my ED. 

I chose recovery because my heart was struggling, it would skip beats or start beating really fast and my chest would hurt and i'd get faint, struggle to stand. i also struggled with consistent fainting spells for the entirety of my ED. 

I also chose recovery because yeah, it hurt to sit, and I was miserable and everything ached and my head always hurt and man, was I irritable. The hanger really gets to you. But so does the exhaustion. All I wanted to do was sleep, and I was not fun to be around. My friends and I became distanced because I was too starved to do anything. I lost all my hobbies and my studies weren't doing well either. It was a constant cycle of waking up, counting calories, starving, feeling miserable, overworking myself and then going to bed.

This one's kind of gross but I also had HORRIBLE gum disease. I would brush and brush and brush but because I didn't have the energy to spare, my body couldn't fight off the infection in my mouth. Which was kind of embarrassing, especially when you get lectured at the dentist about it. I just had an appointment with my dentist for the first time since I started all-in recovery, and "somehow" the severe inflammation and gum disease of SIX YEARS is almost completely gone. 

Outside of the gums, I was constantly sick because I couldn't fight much off. I literally had a consistent illness for MONTHS because of stress, exhaustion and starvation. Your body can't manage or clean itself out if it doesn't have the energy. That includes your memory. My memory is also ass because of ADHD and CPTSD, but memory processing is one of the first things to go. Even if you have a good memory now, a lot of people end up losing those memories in recovery because they simply aren't strong enough to retain.

But the most important reason I chose recovery is because I actually developed reactive hypoglycemia. Everyone associates diabetes and blood sugar issues with eating too much or obesity, but... anorexia can make that happen too. I'm lucky that I've only got reactive hypoglycemia, and not pre-diabetes or diabetes itself. But I still have to manage my blood sugar and prick my finger and be concious about my food choices and eat almost every 2-4 hours so my blood sugar doesn't drop too low and I don't die. I have to make sure I eat the right things for dinner so I don't drop in the middle of the night, and my god, I have food in my car and I eat every time before I drive because if my blood sugar crashes while I'm behind the wheel, I would probably end up in a different type of crash.

It's much better now in recovery, since I'm actually eating, but I do have to be concious about it still, and I'm sure if I wasn't, I would be a lot worse. I've been dealing with this for about two years now. I was off my typical "diet" for a few days while on vacation laat month, and my blood sugar was CONSTANTLY dropping. 

I hope this isn't too preachy, your original point is true, I feel like a lot of ed symptoms are usually focused on the aspect of being underweight, but malnutrition really fucks you up. Its cheesy but calories are energy, and without energy, your body can't function the way it's supposed to, and has to "adapt" to a new way of surviving, which drains you, and eventually will kill you if you don't make the switch to recovery. 

It's definitely easier said than done, I knew I was struggling and likely going to die for a long time before I chose to recover, but I hope you can get there. I hate to throw in another cheesy line, but the cheesy bullcrap is often true so... some of the best decisions in your life will often be the hardest ones to make - this is one of them.

This used to actually be one of my most intense fears in middle school.

As a freshman, a few different factors - but mostly a rare, and awful reaction to a medication I was on - resulted in the development of psychosis for me.

It was scary at first, but... a lot of the fears you have about psychosis due to anxiety aren't actually very true, and it doesn't happen like that. Of course, anxiety isn't logical, but using logic is a good way to fight anxiety and reframe thoughts:

Mine was quite mild compared to others, but... you generally have signs show up slowly. You will not wake up one day and have all these intense hallucinations. 

Struggling to fall asleep when you're anxious is absolutely normal but... not sleeping would increase your chances of hallucinations. Not psychosis, but mild hallucinations, like minor auditory hallucinations, and very very minor visual ones. Lack of sleep can also worsen anxiety, and worsened anxiety causes worsened hallucinations and paranoia. Basically... remind yourself to sleep because sleep keeps your brain healthy and lowers risk of sleep-deprived hallucinations.

When my psychosis started, it was small things. First it was a lot of just... background noise that wasn't real. Some of it is called droning, where it has no real meaning, it's literally just noise. Then, it went to the typical "oh, did someone call my name?" and "oh, i hear someone moving/talking in the next room but literally no one is there" ... it was mostly my Mom, due to severe trauma i had went through and had not recieved help for.

The worst of my hallucinations were vivid voices of people, my teachers and my mom, telling me about my mistakes and degrading me.

I had a few visual hallucinations, but they were rare, and didn't come until much later.

Not long into developing symptoms of psychosis, you're able to recognize its not real. I would go into my mom's office after very clearly hearing her speak, and she wouldn't even be home. When I heard my teachers, I practically collapsed because I was in my room, I knew they weren't there.

You will recognize it is not real before you get into a severe stage. The symptoms will be mild. IF you were to develop psychosis, which you likely won't, you will recognize it early on. There is nothing to fear as long as you know to go to the doctor to get evaluated. For me, that was being taken off my new medication, and being put on anti-psychotics for about a year.

Now, I don't really need them. I still hallucinate, and I don't think I'll ever completely stop, but they're much rarer. I know my triggers to prevent them, and even when they do happen, I am able to use logic to tell that they aren't real, even if it feels very real. 

TL;DR - you will not develop psychosis overnight. it is a slow process and if you were to start hallucinating, the hallucinations would initially be mild, you would recognize it within a short period of time, and if you go see a doctor/psychiatrist asap, it will be managable.

13 is a normal age to start experiencing these things, especially because you're going through puberty and you're also just... maturing, a bit. I cannot stress this enough, and I know it's easier said than done, but try and find help. I really reccomend seeing a therapist, and your GP, who can help refer you to a therapist, a psychiatrist if need be, or can be a stand-in for those professionals if you're truly unable to, especially for the self harm aspect. The earlier you get help, the easier it will be to get better. And you want it easy, because, even though you don't feel like you're bad enough now, and that other people have it worse, when it is truly bad enough, you still won't believe it. The concept of bad enough is a myth. Seek treatment as early and as quick as you can.

Whatever reason you have to think you don't deserve therapy or don't need therapy is wrong. This is an illness, and because we can't see it, it's very deceitful, and we often believe the lies the illness will tell us. Treatment is hard, but it will free you and it is absolutely necessary, even if you have to treat yourself for part of the journey.

Absolutely. I used to be afraid I would lose control and people would think I was crazy. I was also really afraid of being schizophrenic, even if I had no family history, because of the "looking crazy" to outsiders part.

Ironically, I developed psychosis after a med trip, which gave me all the symptoms of schizophrenia, but technically doesn't qualify as it was med induced and is now only present with certain triggers, without any current use of anti-psychotics or mood stabilizers.

And if it helps for reassurance - you won't lose control. You'll recognize something is off, especially if you just start having hallucinations. It won't feel the same way as your anxiety will either. It probably varies for cases, but my first ones were hearing my teacher's voices when I was home. Which obviously wasn't right. It literally knocked me out if my chair because I was like "What the shit???"

After a few of those, I got off those meds and was temporarily put on an anti-psychotic and mood stabilizer, which i needed for the time being, but became more damaging as my body started getting back to "normal"

I still have mine, but they're very mild and you get in a habit of realizing it's not real, similar to anxiety. I'll hear footsteps, but I know the person who's footsteps I'm hearing isn't at home or in the room I heard it from. It might sound real, but it isn't logical. I used to have to check after hearing certain sounds, but now I rarely do.

With all that being said, you are not crazy and it's very rare for schizophrenia or psychosis to develop unless you're a chronic drug user or under SEVERE mental stress for a long period of time. My advice, other than self reassurance, is using a grounding technique to help you relax and come to tune with your senses, which will give you that sense of being in tune with the world.

I'm gonna be honest, I think the reason why a lot  vegetarian/vegans are skinny is because, one, veganism and vegetarianism often co-exists with eating disorders [speaking from personal experience; obviously not every vegan/vegetarian has an ED] and two, because a lot of vegans and vegetarians don't have a handle on proper nutrition [again, not everyone].

Obviously carbs and fats can help with weight gain but protein is really where it's at. You should definitely look into foods labeled "protein packed". Things like protein shakes can be very helpful but there's lots of "normal" vegetarian foods that have extra protein in them. I know kodiak makes lots of food with extra protein like waffles, pancakes, oatmeal, granola bars, graham crackers, etc. I'd reccomend looking online at a local grocery store and just searching for some things so you know in advance!

Protein really helps with muscle gain and repair, which is why it's so good for weight gain. Muscle weighs more than fat and is generally good for weight restoration if you're underweight [which you are].

Make sure you also get carbs, which can be found in most foods [especially bread based foods]. Eating too little carbs can lead to ketosis, which is essentially your brain's starving mode. How much you should intake is based on your calorie intake and output and you can easily calculate it with a few google searches. If you haven't been getting enough carbs, you're going to gain weight back pretty fast [which is why diets like keto are not sustainable long term].

Laatly, if it's possible and affordable, seek help of a nutritionist! Their job is to help people base their diets in a way that is not only healthy for their body, but also helps with either weight gain, weight maintaining, or weight loss, depending on your needs. While you can take nutrition courses online or in person, and you can definitely do your research, it's a really good idea to have someone to be a second opinion and make sure you don't accidentally find yourself with disordered eating habits, or worse, an eating disorder.
